summary:
Team Ignis 9th developed Flame Scope, an interactive website for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It brings together NASA’s microgravity combustion studies so students, educators, and engineers can find relevant evidence without searching through individual reports and test tables.

Users can compare experiments side by side, rank studies by a research question, and trace AI-generated answers back to their sources. The Evidence Map shows which conditions, such as material and airflow, were tested together and where evidence is missing. Kids Lab introduces younger learners to the same science through an interactive gravity slider and games.

Fire can behave differently in microgravity, so understanding the conditions behind each finding matters for spacecraft fire-safety research. Flame Scope makes those findings easier to verify and gives learners a hands-on way to explore why fire behaves differently in space.
details:
We built Flame Scope, an interactive research and learning website for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It brings NASA’s microgravity combustion investigations into one place so researchers, engineers, educators, and students can find relevant experiments and check what the evidence supports.

Users can search studies, compare experiments side by side, and rank investigations by a research question, test conditions, or crew environment. The Evidence Map shows whether conditions such as material and airflow were reported together in a single test, appeared in separate tests, or had no matching record. Users can open the original source to check the match. Ask AI provides cited explanations from retrieved NASA records and flags questions where the available evidence is insufficient.

We built the interface with TypeScript, React, and Three.js and the backend with Python and FastAPI. Our data pipeline reads NASA reports and experiment tables, organizes reported conditions, and indexes source passages in PostgreSQL with pgvector on Supabase. The search combines keyword and semantic matching, and Google Geminidrafts explanations from the retrieved evidence.

We used the same research to build two ways to explore the science. The research dashboard helps users inspect the details behind a finding. Kids Lab lets younger learners move a gravity slider to see how an illustrated flame changes. Quizzes and the Fire Safety Officer missions help learners explore fire prevention, detection, and suppression through play.

We considered source traceability, differences in audience expertise, and gaps in experimental coverage. For example, a study can be relevant to lunar fire safety even when its tests provide no direct evidence at lunar gravity. By making those distinctions visible, Flame Scope helps researchers spend less time locating records and gives educators and students a practical way to connect spacecraft fire science to real experiments.
